title: Java Mastery Test
description: Test your Java fundamentals: JVM memory model, OOP, Generics, Collections, Multithreading, and Spring Boot.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between the JVM Heap and Stack memory in Java?
options: Stack stores local primitive variables and method execution frames; Heap stores all instantiated objects and instance variables
Heap is thread-specific while Stack is shared globally across all threads
Stack memory is managed by the Garbage Collector while Heap is manually freed
Heap stores bytecodes while Stack stores compiled machine binaries
questions.explanation: Each thread has its own Stack for method call frames and local primitives; all objects live on the shared Heap managed by the JVM Garbage Collector.

questions.question: Why is the `String` class immutable in Java?
options: For security, thread-safety, and enabling the String Constant Pool to reuse memory safely without side-effects
Because Java does not support character arrays
To prevent strings from exceeding 255 characters
To allow strings to be executed as bytecode
questions.explanation: Immutability allows String pooling (saving heap memory), guarantees thread safety without synchronization, and protects network/database parameters.

questions.question: What is the difference between an `Interface` with default methods and an `Abstract Class` in Java 8+?
options: A class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one abstract class; abstract classes can have instance state (fields), interfaces cannot
Abstract classes cannot contain concrete methods
Interfaces can have constructors with parameters
There is no difference since Java 8
questions.explanation: Java supports multiple interface inheritance but single class inheritance. Abstract classes maintain state via instance fields, which interfaces cannot.

questions.question: What does the `volatile` keyword guarantee in Java multi-threading?
options: Guarantees visibility of variable changes across threads by reading/writing directly from main memory rather than CPU caches
Guarantees atomic execution of compound operations like `count++`
Locks the entire object from concurrent access
Prevents the garbage collector from reclaiming the variable
questions.explanation: `volatile` ensures memory visibility across CPU cores but does NOT provide mutual exclusion/atomicity for compound non-atomic operations.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of `HashMap.get(key)` in Java on average and worst-case (Java 8+)?
options: Average O(1); Worst-case O(log N) due to red-black balanced tree collision bins
Average O(N); Worst-case O(N^2)
Average O(log N); Worst-case O(N)
Always guaranteed O(1) in all scenarios
questions.explanation: Java 8 converts linked list collision chains to self-balancing Red-Black trees (TreeNode) when bin thresholds exceed 8, improving worst-case from O(N) to O(log N).

questions.question: What is Dependency Injection (DI) in the Spring Framework?
options: A design pattern where object dependencies are injected by the Spring IoC container at runtime rather than instantiated with `new` inside classes
A technique for injecting SQL scripts into database connections
A method to dynamically download JAR dependencies from Maven
An automated unit testing tool for REST APIs
questions.explanation: Spring's Inversion of Control (IoC) container manages bean lifecycles and injects collaborating objects (via `@Autowired` or constructor injection).

questions.question: What is Type Erasure in Java Generics?
options: Generic type parameters (`List<String>`) are replaced with their bounds or `Object` at compile time, retaining no runtime generic type info in bytecode
Deleting unused classes during compilation to save disk space
Converting primitive types to their wrapper objects
Clearing variable values from heap memory
questions.explanation: Java generics maintain backward compatibility with older JVM versions by erasing type parameters during compilation.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Checked` and `Unchecked` exceptions in Java?
options: Checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception) must be declared or handled with try-catch at compile time; Unchecked (subclasses of RuntimeException) do not
Unchecked exceptions crash the computer hardware
Checked exceptions are only thrown by the JVM garbage collector
Unchecked exceptions can only be caught in JUnit tests
questions.explanation: The Java compiler enforces handling for Checked exceptions (e.g. `IOException`, `SQLException`), while RuntimeExceptions (e.g. `NullPointerException`) are unchecked.

questions.question: In Java 8 Streams, what is the difference between intermediate and terminal operations?
options: Intermediate operations (e.g. `filter`, `map`) are lazy and return a new Stream; Terminal operations (e.g. `collect`, `forEach`) trigger computation and produce a result
Terminal operations can be chained indefinitely
Intermediate operations write data to disk
Terminal operations run on separate threads exclusively
questions.explanation: Streams are evaluated lazily: pipeline processing begins only when a terminal operation is invoked.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `@Transactional` annotation in Spring Boot?
options: Automatically wraps method execution in a database transaction, rolling back on unhandled runtime exceptions and committing on success
Encrypts financial payment transactions
Logs all method parameters to a CSV file
Translates SQL queries to MongoDB syntax
questions.explanation: `@Transactional` manages ACID transaction boundaries declaratively, committing upon completion or rolling back if an exception occurs.
